title: Load Balancing
tagline: Spread traffic across servers without creating new failure modes: L4 vs L7, selection algorithms, health checks, draining, global routing and retry storms.

sections.content:
The moment a service runs on more than one machine, something has to decide which machine handles each request. That something is a **load balancer**: a component that sits in front of a pool of identical backends, presents a single address to clients, and spreads work across the pool.

It solves four problems at once:
- **Capacity.** Ten servers can serve roughly ten times the traffic of one. Horizontal scaling only works if traffic is actually spread across them.
- **Availability.** When a server crashes, the load balancer notices through **health checks** and stops sending it traffic. Users see a blip instead of an outage.
- **Operability.** You can take servers out of rotation one at a time to deploy, patch or resize them (**connection draining**), so releases need no downtime.
- **Decoupling.** Clients know one stable name. The fleet behind it can grow, shrink, move between availability zones or change instance types without clients noticing.

Load balancing happens at several layers of a modern stack: **DNS and anycast** pick a region, a **cloud or edge load balancer** terminates TLS and routes HTTP, and inside the cluster a **reverse proxy, sidecar or client library** picks a specific instance for each service-to-service call. The same core ideas apply at every layer: which algorithm picks the backend, how failures are detected, and what happens to in-flight requests.

This chapter covers L4 vs L7 balancing, the selection algorithms (with a simulation that shows why round robin can melt a slow server), health checks, session affinity, TLS termination, draining, global load balancing, the common proxies and cloud products, client-side balancing and service meshes, keeping the load balancer itself from being a single point of failure, and the retry storms that can turn a small failure into a large one.

sections.title: The Restaurant Host
sections.content:
A busy restaurant has a host at the door. Guests never pick their own table or waiter. The host does.

A naive host seats parties strictly in turn: waiter 1, waiter 2, waiter 3, waiter 1... (**round robin**). That works until one waiter is new and slow. Their section fills with unhappy guests while the others stand idle. A better host glances at the floor and seats the next party with whoever currently has the fewest tables (**least connections**). A host with a very large floor can't scan every section, so they glance at two random waiters and pick the less busy one (**power of two choices**). That turns out to be almost as good.

The host also checks on the staff. If a waiter goes home sick, the host stops seating guests in their section (**health checks**). When a waiter's shift ends, the host stops giving them *new* parties but lets them finish serving the tables they have (**connection draining**).

Some regulars insist on the same waiter every visit (**session affinity**). It feels personal, but if that waiter is sick the regular has a bad night, and it makes the sections uneven. Restaurants that keep the order history in a shared system (the kitchen ticket, not the waiter's memory) let any waiter serve anyone.

And a smart restaurant never has just one host. If the only host faints, nobody gets seated, no matter how many waiters are free. The load balancer must not become the single point of failure it was meant to remove.

sections.title: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing
sections.content:
Load balancers are classified by the OSI layer they make decisions at.

**Layer 4 (transport)** balancers see IP addresses, ports and the protocol (TCP/UDP), but not the bytes inside the stream. They pick a backend when a **connection** (or UDP flow) starts, and every packet of that connection goes to the same backend. Implementations either proxy the connection, NAT the packets, or use **direct server return** (DSR, where responses bypass the LB entirely). Because they don't parse HTTP, they are very fast, handle millions of connections, support any TCP/UDP protocol (databases, MQTT, game servers, raw TLS), and add microseconds of latency.

**Layer 7 (application)** balancers terminate the client's connection, parse the request (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, gRPC, WebSocket upgrades), and make a decision **per request**:
- route by host, path, header, cookie or method (`/api/*` → API pool, `/images/*` → image service, `Host: admin.example.com` → admin pool),
- modify requests (add `X-Forwarded-For`, rewrite paths) and responses (headers, compression),
- retry a failed request on another backend, enforce timeouts, rate-limit, run a WAF or authentication,
- balance individual HTTP/2 or gRPC requests multiplexed over one connection, which an L4 balancer cannot split.

| | Layer 4 | Layer 7 |
|---|---|---|
| Decision unit | TCP connection / UDP flow | Each HTTP request |
| Sees | IP, port, protocol (SNI if peeking at TLS) | Full request: URL, headers, cookies, body |
| TLS | Passthrough (or terminate without inspecting) | Terminates, so it can read and route |
| Protocols | Anything over TCP/UDP | HTTP family, gRPC, WebSocket |
| Cost | Very low latency and CPU | More CPU per request, richer features |
| Examples | AWS NLB, Google's Maglev, Meta's Katran, IPVS, HAProxy in TCP mode | AWS ALB, NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy in HTTP mode, Traefik, Cloudflare |

The **long-lived connection problem** shows the difference best. gRPC clients open one HTTP/2 connection and multiplex thousands of RPCs over it. Behind an L4 balancer, each client is pinned to a single backend for the life of that connection, so new backends get almost no traffic after a scale-out. You need an L7 balancer, client-side load balancing, or periodic connection recycling (`max_connection_age` on the gRPC server).

Large systems usually layer both: an L4 tier (anycast + ECMP + something like Maglev) spreads raw connections across a fleet of L7 proxies, which do the per-request routing.

sections.title: Static Algorithms: Round Robin, Weighted and Hash-Based
sections.content:
**Static** algorithms decide without looking at the backends' current load.

**Round robin** sends request *i* to backend *i mod n*. It is simple, stateless apart from one counter, and perfectly fair *if* every backend is equally fast and every request costs the same. Neither is true in practice: request costs vary by orders of magnitude (a cache hit vs a report export), and fleets mix instance types, noisy neighbours and JIT-cold processes. Round robin is the default in NGINX and many other proxies, and it is fine for homogeneous, short, uniform requests.

**Weighted round robin** gives each backend a share proportional to its weight. A backend with weight 2 gets twice the requests of weight 1. NGINX uses a *smooth* weighted round robin that interleaves picks (A A B becomes A B A) instead of sending bursts. Weights work while they stay accurate. They are static configuration, so a backend that slows down because of a GC pause or a bad disk keeps receiving its full share.

**Random** selection behaves like round robin on average, but with more short-term imbalance. Its strength is that it needs no shared state, so many independent balancers can use it without coordinating.

**Hash-based** selection computes `hash(key) mod n` or, better, a consistent hash of a key: the client IP (**IP hash**), a user ID, a URL or a header. The same key always lands on the same backend, which is useful for **cache locality** (each cache shard serves a stable subset of keys) and for stateful protocols. Plain `mod n` remaps almost every key when *n* changes. **Consistent hashing** (see the Consistent Hashing chapter) moves only about 1/n of the keys. **Maglev hashing** (Google, 2016) builds a lookup table that gives near-perfect balance with minimal disruption, and Envoy and Meta's Katran use it. Hashing on client IP is coarse: thousands of users behind one corporate NAT or mobile carrier gateway all hash to the same backend. **Consistent hashing with bounded loads** (HAProxy's `hash-balance-factor`, contributed by Vimeo) caps each backend at, say, 125% of the average and spills the overflow to the next node on the ring.

sections.title: Dynamic Algorithms: Least Connections, Least Response Time and Power of Two Choices
sections.content:
**Dynamic** algorithms use live feedback from the backends.

**Least connections** sends each request to the backend with the fewest active connections or requests in flight. A slow backend accumulates in-flight requests and therefore automatically receives fewer new ones. No configuration is needed, and it is excellent for variable-cost requests and long-lived connections (WebSockets, streaming, uploads). *Weighted* least connections divides by the weight. The weakness is that the balancer needs accurate, current counts, which is easy for one proxy and hard for a fleet of independent balancers that each see only their own traffic.

**Least response time / EWMA** tracks a moving average of each backend's latency (often combined with in-flight count) and prefers the fastest. Linkerd's "peak EWMA" and Finagle use this idea, and NGINX Plus offers `least_time`. It reacts to backends that are slow but not yet overloaded with connections, such as during GC pauses or on a degraded disk.

**Power of two choices (P2C)**: pick **two** backends at random and send the request to the less loaded of the two. This is one of the most useful results in load balancing (Mitzenmacher, 2001). With purely random placement of n requests on n servers, the busiest server ends up with about ln n / ln ln n requests. With two choices it drops to about ln ln n / ln 2. That is an *exponential* improvement from one extra probe.

P2C also fixes a subtle failure of least connections at scale. When many balancers share stale load information, strict least connections makes them **all pick the same "least loaded" backend at the same moment** and overwhelm it (herding). Random sampling breaks the synchronization while still steering away from busy nodes. That is why it is the default "least request" algorithm in Envoy (for unweighted hosts, `choice_count` 2) and in gRPC/Linkerd-style client-side balancers, and why NGINX (`random two least_conn`) and HAProxy (`balance random`, 2 draws by default) offer it.

**Choosing in practice:**
- Homogeneous, uniform, short requests: round robin is fine.
- Mixed instance sizes with stable capacity: weighted round robin.
- Variable request cost or long-lived connections: least connections, or P2C for distributed balancers.
- Need key affinity for cache hits or stateful shards: consistent hashing with bounded load.
- Latency-sensitive RPC between services: P2C with EWMA latency.

The simulation below runs the same Poisson traffic at 85% of total capacity through each algorithm, against two normal backends and one backend that is half as fast.

sections.label: Simulation
sections.explanation: Round robin and random each send about a third of the traffic to the slow backend: 0.71 req/ms against a capacity of 0.5, so its queue grows without bound and mean latency explodes (the number keeps rising if you increase N). Weighted round robin fixes it only because the weights happen to match the speeds exactly. Least connections adapts with zero configuration by watching queue depth, and power of two choices gets most of that benefit while looking at only two backends per decision. The PRNG is seeded, so `node lb-simulation.js` prints exactly these numbers.

sections.title: Health Checks: Active, Passive and Failing Open
sections.content:
A load balancer is only as good as its knowledge of which backends can actually serve.

**Active health checks** probe each backend on a schedule, for example `GET /healthz` every 5–30 s. A backend is marked unhealthy after N consecutive failures (the *unhealthy threshold*) and healthy again after M consecutive successes (the *healthy threshold*). The thresholds add hysteresis so a single dropped probe doesn't flap a server in and out. AWS ALB defaults (instance and IP targets) are a 30 s interval, 5 s timeout, 5 successes to become healthy and 2 failures to become unhealthy. Most teams shorten the interval. Worst-case detection time is roughly interval × unhealthy threshold, plus the timeout.

**Passive health checks** (**outlier detection**) watch real traffic: consecutive 5xx responses, connection resets or timeouts eject a backend for a period that grows on repeated ejections. They react within a few requests rather than a probe interval, and catch failures that a trivial health endpoint misses. Envoy's outlier detection and NGINX's `max_fails`/`fail_timeout` are passive. Open-source NGINX only has passive checks, and active checks are an NGINX Plus feature. HAProxy and Envoy do both, and in production you usually want both.

**What should the health endpoint check?**
- **Liveness** asks "is the process alive and not deadlocked?" A failure means restart it. Keep it trivial.
- **Readiness** asks "should this instance receive traffic right now?" It returns failure during startup (caches cold, migrations not done), while draining, or when the instance is overloaded. Load balancers should use readiness.
- **Avoid deep dependency checks in the LB health check.** If every instance reports unhealthy whenever the shared database is slow, the balancer removes *the entire fleet* at once and turns a degraded service into a total outage. Check the instance's own ability to serve, and let requests fail and report errors for shared dependencies.

**Fail open.** When every backend looks unhealthy, it is usually the health check that is broken, not the whole fleet. AWS ALB and NLB fail open and route to all targets when every target is unhealthy. Envoy has a **panic threshold** (default 50%): if fewer than half the hosts are healthy, it ignores health status and balances across all of them, rather than piling all the traffic onto the few survivors and knocking them over too.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Initial
  Initial --> Healthy : M consecutive probe passes
  Healthy --> Unhealthy : N consecutive probe failures
  Unhealthy --> Healthy : M consecutive probe passes
  Healthy --> Ejected : outlier detection, e.g. 5 consecutive 5xx

sections.title: Session Affinity, and Why to Avoid It
sections.content:
**Session affinity** (sticky sessions) routes every request from the same client to the same backend. L7 balancers do it with a cookie: AWS ALB's `AWSALB` duration cookie, or an application cookie the balancer keys on. L4 balancers do it with source-IP hashing. It exists because some applications keep per-user state, such as a login session, shopping cart or wizard progress, in the memory of the server that created it.

Why it causes trouble:
- **Uneven load.** A few heavy users (or a corporate NAT behind one IP) pin a lot of traffic to one server, and the algorithm can no longer rebalance it.
- **Failures lose state.** When the sticky server dies or is replaced, its users lose their sessions: logged out, carts emptied.
- **Scaling and deploys get worse.** New instances receive only *new* sessions, so a scale-out takes a long time to relieve pressure. Scale-in and rolling deploys must either wait for sessions to expire (long drains) or break them.
- **Hidden coupling.** The application quietly depends on routing behaviour, and the next infrastructure change (new LB, a CDN, multi-region) breaks it.

**The better design is stateless backends**: keep session state in a shared store (Redis, the database) or on the client in a signed, short-lived token (a JWT or encrypted cookie), so any instance can serve any request. This is the same prerequisite for horizontal scaling described in the Scalability chapter.

Legitimate uses remain:
- **WebSockets and other long-lived connections** are naturally sticky for their lifetime, because the connection *is* the affinity. Plan for reconnects to land elsewhere.
- **Cache or shard locality**, such as routing a user to the node that has their data warm, is better done with **consistent hashing** on a key than with cookies. You get locality without hard dependence.
- **Legacy apps you can't change yet.** Use short affinity durations and a plan to remove them.

sections.title: TLS Termination and Preserving Client Identity
sections.content:
Where the encrypted connection ends determines what the balancer can do.

- **TLS termination at the LB**: the balancer holds the certificate, decrypts the traffic, routes on HTTP content, and forwards to backends. It centralizes certificate management (for example AWS Certificate Manager or Let's Encrypt automation), offloads handshake CPU from the app servers, and lets the edge speak HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 to clients while backends speak HTTP/1.1. The traffic from the LB to the backends is plaintext *unless you re-encrypt it*.
- **Re-encryption (TLS bridging)**: terminate, inspect and route, then open a new TLS connection to the backend, often with **mTLS** so both sides authenticate. This is the norm in zero-trust networks and is required by many compliance regimes (PCI DSS, HIPAA environments). Service meshes automate the backend certificates.
- **TLS passthrough**: an L4 balancer forwards the encrypted bytes untouched and the backend terminates. It gives true end-to-end encryption and lets the backend see the client certificate, but no L7 routing is possible. A balancer can still route by **SNI**, the hostname sent in cleartext in the ClientHello, without decrypting. (Encrypted Client Hello, ECH, is starting to hide SNI on the public internet, which reduces what passthrough routers can see.)

**Who is the client?** Once a proxy sits in the middle, the backend's TCP peer is the proxy, not the user. The real client address has to be forwarded explicitly:
- L7: the `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host` headers, or the standardized `Forwarded` header (RFC 7239).
- L4: the **PROXY protocol** (v1 text, v2 binary), a small header prepended to the TCP stream that HAProxy, NGINX, Envoy and AWS NLB understand. NLB can also preserve the client IP directly for instance targets.
- **Security:** `X-Forwarded-For` is just a header that any client can send. Trust it only from your own proxies. Configure the app or framework with the list of trusted proxy hops (NGINX `set_real_ip_from`, Express `trust proxy`) and take the right-most untrusted address. Otherwise attackers can spoof their IP to bypass rate limits and IP allowlists.

sections.title: Connection Draining and Graceful Shutdown
sections.content:
Removing a backend abruptly (for a deploy, a scale-in or a spot-instance reclaim) kills every request it was processing. **Connection draining** (AWS calls it the *deregistration delay*, and its default is 300 s) removes the backend from rotation for **new** requests while letting **in-flight** requests finish, up to a timeout.

Draining needs cooperation from both sides:
1. The orchestrator signals the instance (Kubernetes and ECS send `SIGTERM`) and, around the same time, removes it from the load balancer's target list.
2. **These two happen concurrently and propagate at different speeds.** Endpoint removal can take seconds to reach every proxy and kube-proxy rule. If the app stops accepting connections immediately on SIGTERM, requests routed during that window get "connection refused". The standard fixes are a Kubernetes `preStop` hook that sleeps a few seconds, or having the app fail its readiness check first and keep serving until the LB has noticed.
3. The app then stops accepting new connections, finishes in-flight requests, closes idle keep-alive connections (and sends `Connection: close` / an HTTP/2 GOAWAY on active ones), and exits.
4. A hard deadline (Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, default 30 s) kills the process if draining takes too long. Keep your own timeout below it so you can log what was cut off.

Long-lived connections need their own plan. WebSockets and streaming RPCs may never finish on their own, so tell clients to reconnect (close with a "going away" code, or send GOAWAY), and make clients reconnect with jitter so a deploy doesn't create a reconnect stampede.

Set the drain timeout from your real request latency. Five minutes is far too long for an API whose p99 is 300 ms, and it slows every deploy. It is too short for a 20-minute report export, which should be an async job anyway.

sections.label: Graceful drain
sections.explanation: The order of operations is what matters. On SIGTERM the instance first starts failing `/ready` (the probe during the drain gets 503) but keeps serving, giving the load balancer time to take it out of rotation. Only then does `server.close()` stop accepting connections, and Node waits for the in-flight 300 ms request to complete before the callback exits the process. `closeIdleConnections()` (Node 18.2+) drops idle keep-alive sockets that would otherwise keep the server open. Run with `node` (18+ for global fetch). The output matches the comments.

sections.title: Global Load Balancing: DNS, GeoDNS and Anycast
sections.content:
Inside a region, a load balancer picks a server. Across regions, something has to pick the **region**, to reduce latency (send users to the nearest one) and to survive a region-wide outage.

**DNS-based load balancing** answers the same name with different IP addresses:
- **Round-robin DNS** returns several A/AAAA records. Clients usually try the first one, and many retry the next if it fails. It is crude: there is no health awareness unless the DNS provider adds it.
- **GeoDNS / latency-based routing** answers according to the resolver's location or measured latency. AWS Route 53 offers weighted, latency-based, geolocation, geoproximity, failover, multivalue and IP-based routing policies. Cloudflare, NS1 and Azure Traffic Manager are similar. Health checks remove unhealthy regions from answers.
- **Limits:** DNS decisions are only as fresh as caches allow. The TTL is a request, not a guarantee, so some resolvers and long-running clients (JVMs with old defaults, connection pools) hold on to answers well past it. Failover therefore takes from about one TTL to much longer for some clients. The decision also sees the *resolver's* location, not the user's. EDNS Client Subnet helps where supported, but public resolvers such as Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 don't send it for privacy reasons.

**Anycast** announces the **same IP address** from many locations using BGP, and the internet's routing delivers each packet to the topologically nearest site. Failover happens at the routing layer (withdraw the route and traffic shifts in seconds), with no DNS caching problem. It is how DNS root servers, Cloudflare, Google Cloud's global external Application Load Balancer and AWS Global Accelerator present one IP worldwide. TCP over anycast works because routes are usually stable for a connection's lifetime. When a route changes mid-connection, the new site doesn't know the connection, so providers use connection tracking and consistent hashing to soften this.

**Typical layering in 2026:** anycast or GeoDNS steers users to a nearby edge or region, a regional L7 load balancer spreads requests across zones, and inside the cluster a proxy or mesh picks instances. Each layer health-checks the next, and **failover capacity** must exist: if one of three regions fails, the other two must absorb 50% more traffic each, so plan headroom or degrade deliberately.

sections.title: Reverse Proxies and Cloud Load Balancers
Client-Side Load Balancing and Service Meshes
sections.content:
A central balancer between every pair of services adds a network hop, a capacity bottleneck and a failure domain. For east-west (service-to-service) traffic, many systems move the decision **into the caller**.

**Client-side load balancing**: the client library gets the list of healthy instances from service discovery (DNS SRV, Consul, Eureka, Kubernetes endpoints or an xDS control plane) and picks one per request itself, typically with P2C and latency awareness. gRPC has this built in (`round_robin` and `pick_first` policies, plus **proxyless xDS**). Historically Netflix Ribbon and Twitter Finagle did it. Benefits: no extra hop, per-request balancing of HTTP/2 streams, and decisions informed by the client's own observed latencies. Costs: logic in every language's client library, a discovery system to operate, and every client must be updated to change behaviour.

**Service mesh**: put that logic in a **sidecar proxy** (usually Envoy, or Linkerd's Rust proxy) next to each instance, so applications speak plain HTTP to localhost and the mesh handles balancing, retries, timeouts, mTLS and telemetry uniformly in every language. A **control plane** (Istio, Linkerd, Consul) pushes configuration and certificates to the proxies.

Sidecars cost CPU, memory and a little latency on every hop, so meshes have moved toward lighter data planes. **Istio's ambient mode** (generally available since Istio 1.24, late 2024) replaces per-pod sidecars with a per-node L4 proxy (ztunnel) plus optional per-namespace L7 "waypoint" proxies. **Cilium** implements much of the L4 path in eBPF in the kernel.

When to use what:
- A handful of services in one language: client libraries or plain Kubernetes Services are enough.
- Many services, many languages, compliance requirements for mTLS everywhere, or a need for uniform retries and telemetry: a mesh pays for itself.
- Edge/north-south traffic still goes through an L7 gateway or cloud LB. Meshes manage the inside.

sections.title: Keeping the Load Balancer from Being a Single Point of Failure
sections.content:
A single load balancer in front of fifty servers means the system is only as available as that one box. The balancer tier itself must be redundant.

**Active-passive with a floating IP (VRRP).** Two balancers share a **virtual IP**. The **Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol** (VRRP, RFC 5798), usually via **keepalived**, has the active node send heartbeat advertisements. If they stop, the standby claims the VIP and announces it with gratuitous ARP, and traffic moves in about a second or two. Connections in progress are lost unless connection state is synchronized (`conntrackd`, or HAProxy peers for stick tables). Risks:
- **Split brain**: both nodes think they are active after a network partition. Mitigate with a dedicated heartbeat link, scripts that check the actual health of the proxy process, and fencing.
- Half of the hardware sits idle.
- Most public clouds don't support gratuitous-ARP failover on their virtual networks, so there you move an Elastic/reserved IP through the provider API or use the managed LB.

**Active-active with ECMP and BGP.** Several balancers announce the same VIP to the upstream routers via BGP. The routers spread flows across them with **Equal-Cost Multi-Path** routing, hashing each flow's 5-tuple. If a balancer fails, its route is withdrawn and the flows rehash onto the survivors. All capacity is used and you can scale horizontally. When the set of balancers changes, flows can rehash to a different node, so large-scale L4 balancers (Google's Maglev, Meta's Katran, GitHub's GLB) use consistent hashing and connection tracking so that existing connections survive.

**DNS with multiple LB addresses**: publish several balancer IPs (one per zone) and health-check them. It is simple, but subject to DNS caching delays.

**Managed cloud LBs** are already redundant across availability zones and scale automatically. You still own the configuration: enable multiple AZs with healthy targets in each, check whether cross-zone load balancing is on (always on at the load-balancer level for ALB, though it can be turned off per target group; off by default for NLB), and request pre-warming or capacity reservations for predictable massive spikes.

And remember the dependencies of the LB tier: its DNS records, certificates (an expired cert is an outage), configuration pipeline and control plane. A bad config push to every balancer at once is a global single point of failure, so stage LB config changes like code.

sections.title: Retries, Timeouts and the Thundering Herd
sections.content:
Load balancers and clients retry failed requests, which is often exactly right: a connection reset on one instance shouldn't fail the user's request. But retries add load at precisely the moment the system has the least capacity, and badly designed retries turn a small failure into a large outage.

**Retry amplification.** If each of three layers (browser → gateway → service → database client) retries 3 times, one failing request at the bottom can become 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 attempts. A backend that is struggling at 100% load receives several times its normal traffic and can never recover. That is a **retry storm**, a form of metastable failure, where the system stays down even after the original trigger is gone.

**Thundering herd.** Many clients act in lockstep: all of them retry exactly 100 ms after a shared failure, all reconnect the instant a server comes back, or all expire the same cache key at the same second. The recovering component sees a synchronized spike far above normal traffic. Load balancers create a version of this themselves: under least connections, a brand-new or just-recovered backend has zero connections, so it receives *every* new request until it catches up, often while its caches and JIT are still cold. **Slow start** (AWS ALB slow-start mode, Envoy's slow start, HAProxy's `slowstart`) ramps a new backend's share up over a configured window.

Defences:
- **Exponential backoff with jitter.** Double the delay each attempt up to a cap, and randomize it ("full jitter": sleep a random time between 0 and the backoff), so retries spread out instead of arriving in waves.
- **Retry budgets.** Allow retries only up to a fraction of normal traffic (for example 10% extra), as Envoy and Finagle do, instead of a fixed count per request. During a real outage the budget runs out and requests fail fast.
- **Retry at one layer.** Usually that is the layer closest to the failure that has enough context. Other layers pass errors through.
- **Only retry what is safe.** Idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE), or writes carrying an **idempotency key** the server deduplicates. Never blindly retry a non-idempotent POST that may already have succeeded on a timed-out backend. Many proxies retry only connection failures by default, and that is a sensible default.
- **Timeouts and deadline propagation.** Every call needs a timeout shorter than its caller's. Pass the remaining deadline downstream (gRPC does this natively) so no one works on a request whose client has already given up.
- **Circuit breakers and load shedding.** Stop sending to a failing dependency for a while, and reject excess load early with 503/429 plus `Retry-After`, rather than queueing it until everything times out.
- **Hedged requests** (from Google's "The Tail at Scale") send a second copy of a slow idempotent read after, say, the p95 latency, and use whichever answer arrives first. This cuts tail latency for a few percent of extra load, and should be used within a budget.

sections.label: Backoff & budget
sections.explanation: Without jitter, all 1,000 clients retry at exactly 100, 300 and 700 ms, so the recovering backend gets the entire herd in a single 10 ms window. Full jitter spreads the same retries over time, cutting the peak about 6×. The retry budget caps extra load during a total outage at 10% (500 → 550 requests) instead of the 4× (2,000 requests) that a fixed 3-retries policy would produce. The output is deterministic thanks to the seeded PRNG.

sections.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
sections.content:
- **Round robin across uneven backends or uneven requests.** One slow instance or one expensive endpoint and the queue on that node grows without bound. Prefer least connections or P2C.
- **Health checks that test shared dependencies.** A slow database marks *every* instance unhealthy and the LB removes the whole fleet. Readiness should reflect the instance itself, and load balancers should fail open.
- **Health checks that test nothing.** A `/health` that returns 200 while the app's thread pool is exhausted. Pair active checks with passive outlier detection on real traffic.
- **Sticky sessions as an architecture.** They hide state on servers, unbalance load and lose users on failure. Externalize state, and use consistent hashing when you only need locality.
- **L4 balancing for gRPC/HTTP/2.** Long-lived multiplexed connections pin each client to one backend. Use L7, client-side balancing or connection max-age.
- **Exiting immediately on SIGTERM.** Requests still routed during endpoint propagation fail. Fail readiness, wait, drain, then exit.
- **Drain timeouts copied from defaults** (300 s) that slow every deploy, or set shorter than real request durations.
- **Trusting `X-Forwarded-For` from anyone.** Accept it only from your own proxy hops.
- **Retries at every layer, without backoff, jitter or budgets.** That is a retry storm waiting for its trigger. Retry idempotent operations only, at one layer, within a budget.
- **Forgetting the LB is a component.** A single balancer instance, an unmonitored certificate expiry, or an unstaged config push to every balancer is a single point of failure.
- **No headroom for failover.** Losing one of three zones or regions moves 50% more load onto each survivor. If they run at 80%, failover is an outage.

sections.title: Interview cheat-sheet: picking an algorithm
sections.content: **Round robin**: identical servers, uniform short requests. **Weighted RR**: known, stable capacity differences. **Least connections**: variable request cost, long-lived connections, a single balancer. **Power of two choices**: many independent balancers or client-side LB; it avoids herding on stale data and is the Envoy default. **Least response time / EWMA**: latency-sensitive RPC. **Consistent hashing (bounded load)**: cache or shard locality without sticky cookies. Always pair the algorithm with health checks, slow start for new backends, and retries with backoff, jitter and a budget.

items: A **load balancer** gives clients one stable address and spreads requests across interchangeable backends. It provides capacity, availability through health checks, and zero-downtime operations through draining.

**L4** balancers route whole TCP/UDP connections by IP and port (fast, protocol-agnostic, TLS passthrough). **L7** balancers terminate the connection and route each HTTP/gRPC request by host, path or header. gRPC/HTTP/2 needs L7 or client-side balancing.

**Algorithms:** round robin and weighted RR are static and break when backends or requests are uneven. Least connections and least response time adapt to live load. **Power of two choices** gets near-optimal balance from two random probes and avoids herding across many balancers.

**Consistent hashing** (ring, Maglev, bounded-load variants) gives key affinity for cache locality while moving only about 1/n of keys when backends change. Plain `hash mod n` remaps nearly everything.

**Health checks:** active probes (interval × threshold detection time) plus passive outlier detection on real traffic. Use readiness, not deep dependency checks, and **fail open** when everything looks unhealthy.
**Avoid session affinity:** it unbalances load and loses users on failure. Keep backends stateless (shared session store or signed tokens), and use consistent hashing when you only want locality.

**TLS** terminates at the LB (central certificates, L7 routing), optionally re-encrypting with mTLS to the backends. Forward client identity with X-Forwarded-For/Forwarded or the PROXY protocol, and trust it only from your own proxies.

**Graceful draining:** on SIGTERM, fail readiness, keep serving until the LB notices, stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close idle keep-alives, and exit before the hard deadline. Tune the deregistration delay to real request latency.

**Global LB** picks a region with GeoDNS/latency DNS (limited by caching and TTLs) or **anycast** (one IP announced by BGP, failover at the routing layer). Keep enough headroom to absorb a failed region.

**No SPOF:** run redundant balancers (VRRP/keepalived active-passive with a floating VIP, or ECMP/BGP active-active) or managed multi-AZ cloud LBs. Prevent retry storms with exponential backoff + jitter, retry budgets, idempotency keys, deadlines and slow start.

quiz.question: A gRPC service runs behind an L4 (TCP) load balancer. After scaling from 4 to 8 instances, the 4 new instances receive almost no traffic. What is the most likely reason?
options: L4 load balancers cannot route to more than 4 targets
gRPC multiplexes many requests over long-lived HTTP/2 connections, and an L4 balancer chooses a backend only once per connection
The new instances failed their health checks because gRPC does not support HTTP health probes
L4 balancers always use IP hash, which never selects new instances
quiz.explanation: L4 balancing happens per connection. Existing clients keep their HTTP/2 connections to the original instances, and all their RPCs ride on them. Use an L7 balancer that balances per request, client-side load balancing, or a server-side max connection age so clients reconnect and rebalance.

quiz.question: Three backends sit behind a round-robin balancer. One of them is an older instance type with half the throughput. Under heavy load, what happens?
options: Round robin automatically sends the slow server fewer requests
All three servers slow down equally
The slow server still receives a third of the traffic, which can exceed its capacity, so its queue and latency grow without bound
The balancer marks the slow server unhealthy immediately
quiz.explanation: Round robin ignores load. It sends 1/3 of the requests regardless of how fast each server drains them. If that third exceeds the slow server's capacity, its queue grows indefinitely. Least connections or P2C would route around the growing queue automatically, and weighted RR works only if the weights are correct.

quiz.question: Why do Envoy and many client-side balancers default to 'power of two choices' instead of strict least connections?
options: Sampling two random backends and picking the less loaded one gives near-optimal balance and avoids many balancers herding onto the same apparently least-loaded backend
It guarantees perfectly equal load on every backend
It requires no knowledge of backend load at all
It is the only algorithm compatible with TLS
quiz.explanation: Strict least connections with many independent balancers and stale counts makes them all pick the same backend simultaneously. Random sampling of two breaks that synchronization while still steering away from busy nodes. The maximum load drops exponentially compared with pure random (about ln ln n vs ln n / ln ln n).

quiz.question: The load balancer's health check calls `/health`, which queries the shared primary database. The database has a 30-second latency spike. What is the risk?
options: None, because health checks are ignored during database maintenance
Only one backend will be affected
The health checks will use more database connections, but routing is unaffected
Every backend fails its health check at once, so the load balancer may remove the entire fleet and turn a slowdown into a full outage
quiz.explanation: A shared dependency failing makes all instances look unhealthy simultaneously. Readiness checks should reflect the instance's own ability to serve. Fail-open behaviour (AWS ALB routing to all targets when all are unhealthy, Envoy's panic threshold) exists to limit exactly this failure.

quiz.question: What is the main problem with relying on sticky sessions to keep users' login state in server memory?
options: Sticky sessions only work with Layer 4 load balancers
When the sticky server fails or is scaled in, its users lose their sessions, and load can't be rebalanced away from busy servers
Sticky sessions prevent TLS termination
Browsers reject load balancer cookies
quiz.explanation: Affinity hides state on individual servers, which makes failures user-visible (logouts, lost carts), skews load, and slows scaling and deploys. Store sessions in a shared store or signed tokens so any instance can serve any request.

quiz.question: A Kubernetes pod exits immediately on SIGTERM, and during every deploy a few requests fail with connection refused. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the number of replicas
Switch the load balancer to IP hash
On SIGTERM, fail readiness and keep serving briefly (or use a preStop sleep) until endpoint removal propagates, then stop accepting, drain in-flight requests and exit
Disable health checks during deploys
quiz.explanation: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen concurrently, and proxies learn about the removal a few seconds later. Requests routed in that window hit a closed socket. Delaying the close until the LB has noticed, then draining, eliminates the errors.

quiz.question: Your backend reads the client IP from `X-Forwarded-For` to enforce per-IP rate limits. What must you ensure?
options: Only trust X-Forwarded-For entries added by your own known proxies, because clients can send arbitrary values in that header
Always use the left-most address in the header
Switch to HTTP/1.0 so the header cannot be forged
Nothing, because the header is set by the browser and cannot be modified
quiz.explanation: Any client can send an X-Forwarded-For header. Configure the trusted proxy hops (Express `trust proxy`, NGINX `set_real_ip_from`) and use the right-most address that was not added by your own infrastructure. Otherwise attackers spoof IPs to bypass rate limits and allowlists.

quiz.question: Why does DNS-based failover between regions often take much longer than the configured TTL for some users?
options: DNS records cannot be changed while users are connected
Some resolvers and long-running clients cache answers beyond the TTL, and existing connections keep using the old IP
TTLs are measured in hours by the DNS protocol
GeoDNS only updates once per day
quiz.explanation: TTL is advisory. Some resolvers clamp or ignore it, and applications (older JVM defaults, connection pools, keep-alive connections) keep using resolved addresses. Anycast avoids this by failing over at the BGP routing layer, behind an unchanged IP.

quiz.question: Two HAProxy nodes share a virtual IP using keepalived (VRRP). What does this design primarily protect against, and what is its main risk?
options: It protects against DDoS attacks, and the risk is higher latency
It protects against backend failures, and the risk is uneven load
It doubles throughput, and the risk is TLS certificate conflicts
It removes the single load balancer as a point of failure, and the risk is split brain, where both nodes claim the VIP during a partition
quiz.explanation: VRRP moves the virtual IP to the standby when the active node's advertisements stop. If the nodes can't see each other but both are alive, both may claim the VIP (split brain). Use dedicated heartbeat links, health-checking scripts and fencing. Active-passive also leaves the standby's capacity idle.

quiz.question: After a brief outage, 1,000 clients all retry exactly 100 ms, 300 ms and 700 ms after their first failure. What best prevents this from overwhelming the recovering service?
options: Reduce the backoff base to 10 ms so retries finish sooner
Increase the retry count so each client is more likely to succeed
Add random jitter to the backoff and cap total retries with a retry budget
Retry non-idempotent POSTs as well, so fewer requests are lost
quiz.explanation: Synchronized retries form a thundering herd that arrives in waves. Full jitter spreads them over time, and a retry budget limits the extra load during a real outage, which prevents a retry storm. Faster or more retries make the herd worse, and retrying non-idempotent writes risks duplicate side effects.
